newsitem.title: ITALY: Sicilian boss Aglieri stays mum under arrest.
newsitem.headline: Sicilian boss Aglieri stays mum under arrest.

text.p: Mafia boss Pietro Aglieri refused to co-operate on Tuesday when Italian investigators tried to question him for the first time since his arrest last week, justice sources said.

Aglieri, the suspected number two in the Mafia hierarchy, was visited in the top security wing of Ucciardone jail in the Sicilian capital Palermo by two magistrates probing the mob murder in 1980 of Sebastiano Pipitone, a Sicilian bookseller.
The meeting lasted only a few minutes after Aglieri said he would not answer questions, the sources said.
Aglieri, 38, was captured with two alleged Mafia hitmen in a police raid on a Sicilian farmhouse last Friday in an operation hailed by the authorities as a major blow to organised crime.
Nicknamed "U Signurinu" (The Young Gentleman) in Sicilian dialect for his supposed elegance, Aglieri had been on the run since December 1989.

The discovery in his hideout of an elaborate chapel and several theological texts indicated that Aglieri had become a devout Roman Catholic while on the run and led to speculation that he might turn state's evidence once arrested.
His lawyer, Rosaria Di Gregorio, told Italian television on Tuesday that her client would not become a turncoat or dissociate himself from mob activites.
"Dissociation is a very severe mental illness," she said.
She said she had asked a court to release the theological and philosophical texts seized during the arrest.
Aglieri's capture was the most important Mafia arrest since that of Sicilian boss Giovanni Brusca last year.
Italy's most wanted man is fugitive boss Bernardo Provenzano but Aglieri has ranked close behind him since the capture in 1993 of "boss of bosses" Salvatore 'The Beast' Riina.
Italian police said on Tuesday that a further blow fell on Riina's empire with the arrest in the French port of Toulon of Francesco Albamonte, a suspected leading lieutenant of Riina.
Albamonte, 35, was arrested in an operation mounted with Italian police help at a petrol station where he stopped to refuel his car, police said.

Aglieri has been sentenced in absentia to life for the murder of octagenarian boss Benedetto Grado, although that has yet to become definitive in Italy's exhaustive appeals procedure, and 12 years for drug trafficking.

He stands accused of involvement in the car bomb killings of magistrates Paolo Borsellino and Giovanni Falcone in 1992 as well as of former European parliamentarian Salvo Lima who was gunned down in the same year.
